column3: Question
column4: Correct answer
column5: Why it is correct
column6: Why the tempting wrong answer is wrong

column3: A word appears in every document in the corpus. What is its IDF?
column4: Zero, so it contributes nothing to ranking
column5: IDF is log(N/df). When df equals N that is log(1) which is exactly 0, so the term drops out of the score entirely.
column6: People guess 'maximum' because the word is everywhere. Frequency across documents is what KILLS the signal, not what creates it. This is a free stopword list built into the maths.

column3: What actually makes an inverted index fast at query time?
column4: Cost tracks the matches, not the corpus size
column5: The index is built once at ingestion. At query time you jump straight to the posting list for that word, so work scales with the number of matches.
column6: 'Scans in parallel' is the trap: parallel scanning is still reading the whole corpus. The win is not reading it at all.

column3: Why does TF-IDF score zero for 'car crash' when you search 'automobile accident'?
column4: It matches character strings, not meaning
column5: TF-IDF is purely lexical. It compares character strings, and these two phrases share none, so every term contributes zero.
column6: Nothing is wrong with the documents or the stemmer. The method itself has no concept of meaning. That gap is the entire reason embeddings exist.

column3: BM25 adds term saturation on top of TF-IDF. What does that fix?
column4: The 50th hit should not count like the 1st
column5: Raw TF grows linearly, so a word appearing 50 times scores 50 times higher. BM25's k1 makes extra occurrences give diminishing returns.
column6: Length normalisation is real but that is the b parameter, not saturation. Keep the two straight: k1 saturates frequency, b handles length.

column3: What does the b parameter in BM25 control?
column4: How strongly document length is normalised
column5: b sets how hard long documents are penalised. Finding a rare word in a short document means more than finding it in a 50,000 word one.
column6: Saturation of term frequency is k1, not b. Mixing up the two is the single most common BM25 slip in interviews.

column3: Why prefer cosine similarity over Euclidean distance for text embeddings?
column4: It compares direction and ignores length
column5: Vector length tracks things like word frequency and document length. Cosine measures only the angle, so meaning survives a long and a short text saying the same thing.
column6: Euclidean works fine in high dimensions mathematically. The problem is not that it breaks, it is that it punishes length differences you do not care about.

column3: Word2Vec gives 'bank' a single vector. What does that cost you?
column4: River bank and money bank share one vector
column5: Word2Vec embeddings are static: one vector per word for life, regardless of the sentence around it. Polysemy is unrepresentable.
column6: Nothing about vocabulary size or labels is the issue. This specific limitation is what self-attention was built to solve.

column3: What problem does negative sampling solve when training Word2Vec?
column4: Full-vocabulary softmax is too expensive
column5: The naive update needs a softmax over the whole vocabulary on every step. Negative sampling replaces it with a binary real-or-noise choice over a handful of samples.
column6: It is a compute optimisation, not a quality fix for rare words. The embeddings stay meaningful because telling real context from noise still forces real co-occurrence learning.

column3: How can FastText embed a word it never saw during training?
column4: It composes it from character n-grams
column5: FastText trains on character n-grams, so an unseen word is assembled from sub-word pieces it does know. This is why it survives typos and rich morphology.
column6: There is no dictionary lookup and no random fallback. If you said 'copies the nearest word' you are describing a different system entirely.

column3: Skip-gram or CBOW for rare words, and why?
column4: Skip-gram, each centre word drives more updates
column5: Skip-gram predicts context from one centre word, so each occurrence of a rare word generates several focused training examples.
column6: CBOW averages the surrounding context, which drowns out the rare word's own signal. CBOW is faster and better on frequent words, which is the opposite trade.

column3: In self-attention, what does the Key vector represent?
column4: What a token advertises to be matched against
column5: Key is the label a token advertises so other tokens can match against it. Query is what a token is looking for, Value is what gets passed on.
column6: Mixing up Query and Key is the classic slip. Say it as a room of people: Query is your question, Key is everyone's name badge, Value is what they actually tell you.

column3: Why are attention scores divided by the square root of d_k?
column4: Big dot products saturate softmax, killing gradients
column5: Dot products grow with dimension. Large values push softmax into a near one-hot regime where gradients vanish and learning stalls.
column6: This has nothing to do with positions or parameter count. It is purely about keeping softmax in a range where it still has useful gradients.

column3: What does multi-head attention buy over one single larger head?
column4: Heads specialise in different relations in parallel
column5: Each head has its own projections, so heads can specialise in different relationships at once, such as syntax in one and coreference in another.
column6: It does not replace the feed-forward layer or change the context window. One big head has to collapse every relationship type into a single pattern.

column3: With no positional encoding, how does a Transformer see its input?
column4: As an unordered set, so word order is lost
column5: Attention is permutation invariant. Without position information 'the cat sat' and 'sat cat the' produce identical representations.
column6: The model still runs, which is what makes this subtle. It runs and silently loses all word order.

column3: What does RoPE encode that absolute sinusoidal encodings do not?
column4: Relative position, by rotating Q and K
column5: RoPE rotates Q and K by a position-dependent angle, so the attention score depends on the distance between two tokens rather than their absolute slots.
column6: Absolute sinusoidal encodings give each position its own fixed signal. Relative position is what generalises better to longer sequences.

column3: Architecturally, how do BERT and GPT differ?
column4: BERT attends both ways, GPT only to the past
column5: BERT is encoder-only with bidirectional attention, trained with masked language modelling. GPT is decoder-only with causal attention, trained on next-token prediction.
column6: If you reversed them, remember it this way: GPT generates, so it must not see the future. BERT classifies, so it may see everything.

column3: A Transformer block has attention and a feed-forward net. What does the FFN do?
column4: Transforms each token on its own, after mixing
column5: Attention moves information between tokens. The FFN then transforms each token position independently, and research traces a lot of stored factual knowledge to those weights.
column6: If you said it mixes tokens, you described attention. Keep the division clean: attention routes across the sequence, FFN transforms per token.

column3: What did GPT-3 demonstrate that earlier GPT models did not?
column4: Learning a task from prompt examples alone
column5: Few-shot in-context learning at scale. Put two or three examples in the prompt and the model generalises with zero weight updates.
column6: GPT-2 already showed zero-shot behaviour, so 'learning from the prompt' is the distinguishing jump, not the invention of attention or tokenizers.

column3: What is the correct order of the three RLHF stages?
column4: SFT, then reward model, then PPO
column5: Supervised fine-tuning on human demonstrations, then a reward model trained on human rankings, then PPO optimising against that reward.
column6: Every wrong option puts PPO before the thing it optimises against. You cannot run RL before you have a reward signal to maximise.

column3: What is the KL penalty in RLHF guarding against?
column4: Drifting off SFT until output quality collapses
column5: It keeps the policy close to the SFT model. Without it the policy finds degenerate text that games the reward model while reading terribly.
column6: This is reward hacking, not a memory or tokenizer issue. If a team says they removed the KL term to get higher reward, that is the bug, not the win.

column3: Compared with RLHF, what does DPO remove?
column4: The reward model and the RL loop
column5: DPO shows the optimal RLHF policy has a closed form, so you can train directly on preference pairs and delete both the reward model and the RL loop.
column6: It still needs preference data and still starts from a fine-tuned model. What goes away is the machinery in the middle, not the data.

column3: In Constitutional AI, where does most safety feedback come from?
column4: The model critiquing itself against principles
column5: The model critiques its own output against a written constitution and revises it. Those AI-generated preferences then drive training.
column6: The whole point is removing the human from the per-example loop, because human labelling is the bottleneck. Humans write the principles, not the labels.

column3: Labellers preferred 1.3B InstructGPT over 175B GPT-3. What does that show?
column4: Alignment can beat raw scale on usefulness
column5: Alignment and raw scale are different levers. A much smaller aligned model was preferred around 85% of the time.
column6: This does not mean scale is irrelevant or that small is always better. It means being useful is not the same property as being capable.

column3: What are emergent abilities in large language models?
column4: Skills that appear suddenly past a certain scale
column5: Capabilities almost absent at small scale that appear sharply past a size threshold, like multi-step arithmetic or chain-of-thought reasoning.
column6: They are not programmed in or toggled on. The engineering consequence is that you cannot extrapolate what a 70B model will do from testing a 7B one.

column3: Why do language models hallucinate so confidently?
column4: They optimise plausible next tokens, not truth
column5: They are trained to predict the most plausible next token, and nothing in that objective rewards being right or signals 'I do not know'.
column6: Bad training data and high temperature make it worse but are not the root cause. A perfectly trained model at temperature zero still has no truth check, which is why RAG and citations exist.

column3: What is the correct decoding order?
column4: Temperature, top-k, top-p, then sample once
column5: Temperature reshapes the distribution first, then top-k and top-p cut the tail, then you draw a single sample.
column6: Sampling before filtering means you already picked a token, so the filters do nothing. This is a real production bug, not a theoretical one.

column3: Why does BPE beat a pure word-level vocabulary?
column4: Unseen words split into known sub-words
column5: Any unseen word decomposes into sub-words that are in the vocabulary, so there is no out-of-vocabulary token.
column6: Word-level actually produces SHORTER sequences, so that option is backwards. The trade you accept with BPE is more tokens for full coverage.

column3: Top-k is 40 and the model is very confident. What is the risk?
column4: You still sample from 39 near-zero options
column5: Top-k keeps a fixed count regardless of confidence. If one token holds most of the mass, you are still drawing from 39 near-zero options.
column6: It does not force the top token, which is exactly the danger. Fixed k ignores how sure the model actually is.

column3: What does top-p sampling do that top-k cannot?
column4: Varies how many tokens survive with confidence
column5: Top-p keeps the smallest set reaching cumulative probability p, so the candidate count shrinks when the model is confident and grows when it is unsure.
column6: It is not deterministic, that would be greedy decoding at temperature zero. Top-p adapts the cut, it does not remove randomness.

column3: Why does a long prompt suffer from 'lost in the middle'?
column4: Models attend best to the start and the end
column5: Models attend most reliably to the beginning and end of a long context. Content in the middle can be effectively ignored even though it was retrieved.
column6: Nothing is truncated or compressed. The text is present and the model simply under-attends to it, which is why reranking matters.

column3: 3,000 tokens a query, 10,000 queries a day, $5 per 1M input tokens. Monthly input cost?
column4: About $4,500
column5: 3,000 x 10,000 = 30M tokens a day. At $5 per million that is $150 a day, so about $4,500 a month for input alone.
column6: The common slip is dropping a zero. Do it in two steps: tokens per day first, then dollars per day, then times thirty.

column3: A 7B model is about 28GB in FP32. Roughly what does 4-bit quantization give?
column4: About 3.5GB
column5: FP32 is 4 bytes a weight, 4-bit is half a byte, so you divide by eight. 28GB becomes about 3.5GB.
column6: 14GB is FP16 and 7GB is INT8. Those are all real numbers for different precisions, which is what makes this worth getting right.

column3: In the tag Q4_K_M, what does Q4 mean?
column4: Four bits are used per weight
column5: Four bits per weight. K is the K-quant grouping method and M is the medium size variant balancing accuracy against speed.
column6: Nothing in the tag refers to GPUs, context length or version number. Each letter is about how weights are stored.

column3: What is the real engineering argument for running a model locally?
column4: Data stays put and tokens cost nothing
column5: Data never leaves the machine, it works offline, and there is no per-token bill. You pay in RAM and accept a quality gap.
column6: Local does not beat frontier quality, and claiming it does in an interview will cost you. The honest answer names the trade.

column3: What is the practical test of whether a local model is usable?
column4: It must fit in RAM or VRAM, or it crawls
column5: The weights must fit entirely in RAM or VRAM. Once it pages to disk, speed collapses below anything interactive.
column6: Parameter count alone does not decide it, because quantization changes the footprint. Fit is the rule, not size.

column3: A document dwarfs the context window. What does map-reduce do?
column4: Summarise each chunk, then combine the summaries
column5: Map: process each chunk independently and summarise it. Reduce: combine those summaries into the final answer. Chunks can run in parallel.
column6: Truncating loses content and context windows are fixed at inference. The alternative is refine, which is sequential and slower but keeps cross-chunk coherence.

column3: In the universal chat format, what is the system role for?
column4: Behaviour and limits for the whole conversation
column5: System sets persona, behaviour and constraints for the whole conversation. User is a human turn, assistant is a model turn.
column6: It is not metadata and the model certainly does not ignore it. Replaying prior assistant turns is how you give a stateless API memory.

column3: When is few-shot strictly better than zero-shot?
column4: When code must parse an exact output shape
column5: When code downstream must parse the output. Zero-shot returns 'Positive', 'positive', 'POSITIVE' and sentences; examples lock one exact string.
column6: Few-shot costs MORE tokens, so cost is never the reason. You pay those tokens to buy format reliability.

column3: Why does chain-of-thought help on multi-step problems?
column4: Intermediate tokens give later steps context
column5: Generating intermediate steps gives the model more relevant context for each subsequent decision instead of jumping straight to an answer.
column6: It does not change weights or disable sampling. It changes what is in the context when the final token is chosen.

column3: In DSPy, how does BootstrapFewShot differ from LabeledFewShot?
column4: It keeps only demos that passed your metric
column5: Bootstrap runs the model on training examples, scores them with your metric, and keeps only the ones that passed.
column6: LabeledFewShot is the one that picks at random. Neither touches instruction wording, which is what MIPROv2 adds.

column3: What can MIPROv2 optimise that BootstrapFewShot cannot?
column4: The instruction wording itself
column5: MIPROv2 searches over instruction phrasing as well as examples, using Bayesian optimisation to explore candidate wordings.
column6: No DSPy optimizer touches weights, the tokenizer or embedding size. They all operate on the prompt.

column3: What makes GEPA different from the earlier DSPy optimizers?
column4: It reflects on its own failures and rewrites
column5: GEPA reflects on its own failed outputs and rewrites the prompt from what went wrong, rather than only selecting among examples.
column6: Bootstrap selects demos and MIPROv2 searches instruction wording. None of them, GEPA included, touch the model's weights.

column3: Your bot forgot the user's name from two turns ago. Root cause?
column4: The API is stateless, history was not resent
column5: Chat APIs are stateless. The model sees only what you send on this call, so prior turns must be resent every time.
column6: Nothing was deleted by the provider. If your bot remembers, it is because you stored and resent history, or added a checkpointer.

column3: What does the pipe operator in LCEL actually do?
column4: Feeds one Runnable's output into the next
column5: It composes Runnables: the output of the left becomes the input of the right. Prompt formats, model generates, parser extracts.
column6: It is sequential composition, not concurrency and not caching. Everything in the chain implements one shared interface.

column3: Total generation time is unchanged. Why stream anyway?
column4: First token lands fast, so it feels quicker
column5: Time to first token drops to under a second, so perceived speed improves several-fold even with identical total time. Users can also stop early.
column6: You are billed for the same tokens either way. The win is entirely in perception and control.

column3: You swap ChatOpenAI for ChatAnthropic. Why does the rest of the chain survive?
column4: Both implement the same Runnable interface
column5: Every chat model wrapper implements the same Runnable interface, so the prompt and parser either side are unaffected. It is a one-line change.
column6: LangChain does not rewrite your prompt or translate key formats. The abstraction is the shared interface, nothing more.

column3: What is MessagesPlaceholder for in a ChatPromptTemplate?
column4: A slot where conversation history is injected
column5: It reserves a slot in the template where a list of prior messages gets injected at runtime, which is how multi-turn history enters the prompt.
column6: It is not a fallback or a cache. Without it you would have to rebuild the whole message list by hand on every single turn.

column3: What counts as a valid stop condition for an autonomous coding goal?
column4: A command with exact expected output
column5: Something a machine can evaluate: a shell command plus its exact expected output, such as pytest exiting 0 and printing '12 passed'.
column6: 'The code looks good' cannot be evaluated, so the loop either never ends or ends on a guess. That is how agents report success on broken code.

column3: When do you want a repeating loop rather than a one-shot goal?
column4: When work recurs and has no finish line
column5: When the work recurs and has no finish line, like a test watcher or a quality monitor. A goal ends, a loop runs until you stop it.
column6: Task size is irrelevant. A huge task with a clear finish line is still a goal.

column3: Your agent edited three files and declared success. No tests ran. What failed?
column4: There was no verifiable stop condition
column5: There was no verifiable stop condition, so 'done' was the agent's own judgement rather than a check you defined.
column6: Model size is not the issue. Give it a command that must pass and a turn cap, and this cannot happen.

column3: Your chunks are too small. What typically breaks?
column4: One answer splits across chunks and is lost
column5: A single answer gets split across chunk boundaries, so no individual chunk carries the whole fact and retrieval returns fragments.
column6: Nothing technical fails. Embeddings and BM25 work normally, which is why this is hard to spot without evaluating.

column3: Why add overlap between adjacent chunks?
column4: A sentence cut by a boundary still survives
column5: Overlap means a sentence cut by a boundary still appears intact in one of the two chunks.
column6: It increases storage rather than reducing it. You are deliberately paying duplication to protect boundary content.

column3: A user searches the code ERR-4042. Why does dense-only retrieval miss it?
column4: Embeddings blur rare exact strings
column5: Embeddings capture semantics. Rare exact strings like error codes and SKUs have little semantic signal, so they get blurred against similar-looking codes.
column6: Dense retrieval does not ignore numbers wholesale. It just has no reason to treat this exact string as distinctive, which is where BM25 wins.

column3: What does Reciprocal Rank Fusion actually combine?
column4: Rank positions from each list, not raw scores
column5: RRF sums 1/(k + rank) across lists. It uses rank position only, so you never have to make BM25 scores and cosine scores comparable.
column6: Combining raw scores is exactly what RRF avoids, because those scores are on incompatible scales.

column3: Why can a cross-encoder not replace your first-stage retriever?
column4: Nothing can be precomputed, so it scores every pair
column5: A bi-encoder embeds chunks once at ingestion. A cross-encoder must run the model on every query-document pair, so a million chunks means a million forward passes per question.
column6: It is MORE accurate, not less. Accuracy is why you use it on the top 50, and cost is why you cannot use it on everything.

column3: You pass 10 chunks and the right one sits 6th. What is the risk?
column4: It lands mid-context where attention is weakest
column5: Mid-context content gets the least reliable attention, so retrieval technically succeeded while the answer still comes out wrong.
column6: Nothing discards it. The chunk is right there in the prompt and under-used, which is why reranking into the top few matters.

column3: RAGAS faithfulness is low but answer relevance is high. What happened?
column4: It sounds on-topic but the context does not support it
column5: The answer is on-topic but makes claims the retrieved context does not support. That is the textbook signature of RAG hallucination.
column6: High relevance tells you retrieval and topic matching worked. The failure is in generation drifting beyond its evidence.

column3: How does conversation memory differ from RAG?
column4: Memory holds dialogue state, RAG fetches documents
column5: Memory carries dialogue state across turns via a thread and checkpointer. RAG fetches documents for the current question. Production bots need both.
column6: They are not interchangeable. Memory without RAG still invents policy; RAG without memory forgets what you said one turn ago.

column3: A retrieved document contains 'ignore your previous instructions'. What is this?
column4: Indirect prompt injection via the knowledge base
column5: Indirect prompt injection. The attack arrives inside retrieved content rather than from the user, which is why input filtering alone misses it.
column6: This is not a chunking or encoding artefact. Treat retrieved text as untrusted data, never as instructions.

column3: Recall at 50 is excellent but answers are still poor. Where do you look first?
column4: Ordering and how much context you pass
column5: Good recall means the right chunk is in the candidate pile, so retrieval is not the bug. Look at ordering and how much you stuff into the prompt.
column6: Swapping the embedding model or vector database changes retrieval, which you just proved is working. Fix ranking and context size instead.

column3: What does a recursive character splitter do that fixed-size splitting does not?
column4: Break on paragraph and sentence boundaries first
column5: It tries natural boundaries in order, paragraph then sentence then word, and only falls back to a hard cut. Chunks end up uneven but semantically whole.
column6: Equal-size chunks are exactly what fixed-size splitting gives you, and exactly what cuts sentences in half. Uneven is the feature here.

column3: You need a vector store running locally in a notebook with no setup. Which fits?
column4: FAISS or Chroma, both run in-process
column5: FAISS and Chroma run in-process with no server, which is why they work in Colab. Chroma also persists to disk easily.
column6: Pinecone is managed and needs an API key and network. A plain SQL database has no vector index or similarity search without an extension.

column3: SPLADE is called a learned sparse retriever. What does that mean?
column4: It learns sparse term weights with a model
column5: SPLADE predicts a sparse weight over vocabulary terms, including terms not literally in the text, so you get BM25-style exact matching plus some vocabulary expansion.
column6: It is not a small dense encoder. Sparse here describes the vector, most entries being zero, not how the files are stored.

column3: RAGAS and DeepEval both score a RAG system. What do they share?
column4: Both use an LLM as judge against your context
column5: Both use an LLM as a judge, comparing the answer against the retrieved context to produce metrics like faithfulness without hand-labelled ground truth.
column6: That is the appeal and the caveat: no human labels needed, but your scores inherit the judge model's own biases.

column3: Your PDF has charts the text layer never describes. What does multimodal RAG add?
column4: A vision model describes images so they index
column5: A vision model looks at the image or the rendered page and writes a description, which gets embedded and indexed alongside the text.
column6: Larger chunks cannot help, because the information was never in the text layer. Dropping images loses the data entirely.

column3: Retrieval comes back with nothing relevant. What should a production bot do?
column4: Refuse, and say it is not in the sources
column5: Refuse and say so. A grounded bot that cannot find support should decline rather than fill the gap from memory.
column6: Answering from model knowledge is exactly the hallucination RAG was built to stop. Returning the nearest chunk anyway is how wrong policy reaches a customer.

column3: What problem does MCP solve for agents?
column4: One standard way to expose tools to any client
column5: Before MCP, every tool needed bespoke glue per framework. MCP is one protocol, so a server you write once works with any compliant client.
column6: It does nothing to context size or retrieval. Think of it as a standard plug, which is the analogy used in the session.

column3: When is a graph worth the complexity over a straight chain?
column4: When you need branching, retries, cycles or a pause
column5: When control flow is the product: branching, retries, cycles, or pausing for a human. A single prompt with no tools does not need one.
column6: Prompt length and provider count have nothing to do with it. Calling one tool does not justify a graph either.

column3: What does a checkpointer give a LangGraph application?
column4: Saved state, so a run resumes after a pause
column5: It persists graph state after each step, which is what makes pause and resume, conversational memory and crash recovery possible.
column6: It does not speed anything up or add retrieval. It adds durability, which is what lets a run survive a restart.

column3: You resume an interrupted graph under a new thread_id. What happens?
column4: The paused state is not found, it starts fresh
column5: thread_id is the key the checkpoint is stored under. A new id points at no saved state, so the run begins from scratch and the pause context is gone.
column6: Checkpoints never merge across threads. This is the most common human-in-the-loop bug in practice.

column3: What problem does the supervisor pattern solve?
column4: One agent with too many tools picks wrong
column5: A single agent holding twenty tools picks the wrong one. A supervisor routes to narrow specialists that each keep a small, clear toolset.
column6: It is about routing and tool confusion, not streaming or context limits.

column3: What is the loop in the ReAct pattern?
column4: Thought, then Action, then Observation, repeat
column5: Thought, Action, Observation, then around again. The model reasons, calls a tool, reads the result, and decides what to do next.
column6: The observation step is the part people drop. Without feeding the tool result back in, the model is guessing rather than reacting.

column3: How does Tree of Thoughts differ from plain chain-of-thought?
column4: It explores several branches and compares them
column5: Chain-of-thought follows one line of reasoning. Tree of Thoughts branches into several candidate paths, evaluates them and keeps the strongest.
column6: It costs more tokens, not fewer. You spend that budget to escape a single bad opening step.

column3: Your agent answers wrongly after six tool calls. What does tracing give you?
column4: Every step and payload, so you see where it broke
column5: A full record of every step: prompts, tool arguments, returned values and timings, so you can see exactly which call went wrong.
column6: Tracing is observability, not repair. It tells you where to look, then you fix the prompt, the tool or the routing yourself.

column3: In an agent harness, what separates a tool from a skill?
column4: A tool runs code, a skill is guidance it reads
column5: A tool is callable code with arguments and a return value. A skill is procedural guidance the agent loads and reads, usually markdown.
column6: If you reversed them: tools execute, skills steer. An agent ignoring a standing rule is a skill-following failure, not a tool bug.

column3: Why give an agent a file system instead of only a chat history?
column4: Work persists and survives the context window
column5: Files let work persist beyond the context window and be revisited, so long tasks survive compaction and the agent has somewhere to think.
column6: It has nothing to do with speed, and chat history obviously holds text. The difference is durability and structure.

column3: When would you pick an agent harness over hand-writing a LangGraph?
column4: File tools and standing rules already fit the job
column5: When file tools, standing instructions and skills already cover the workflow, so you are not writing a new node for every small behaviour change.
column6: If you need tight explicit control of every branch, write the graph. A harness deliberately hides that control.

column3: A manager asks for last week's revenue. Which path should the router take?
column4: A read-only SQL query against the tables
column5: Revenue is a number in a table, so it comes from a read-only SQL query. Numbers must never be generated from prose or memory.
column6: RAG over policy documents would invent a figure that sounds plausible. Keeping facts in SQL and policy in documents is the rule.

column3: Why must the model never issue mutating SQL on its own?
column4: A wrong generated write damages real data
column5: A generated UPDATE or DELETE hits real data with no review step. Writes go behind a human approval gate, which is what interrupt gives you.
column6: Databases will happily run model-written SQL, which is precisely the danger. Speed and context length are irrelevant here.

column3: A customer asks what the allergen policy says. Which source is correct?
column4: The policy documents, retrieved and cited
column5: Policy wording lives in documents, so retrieve it and cite the source. The citation is what lets a human verify the answer.
column6: The orders table holds transactions, not policy. Model memory is exactly what you are trying to stop it using.

column3: Dining Bot parses generated SQL before running it. Why?
column4: To prove it is SELECT-only before it runs
column5: The query is parsed and checked to be a SELECT before it reaches the database, so a generated INSERT, UPDATE or DROP is rejected rather than executed.
column6: This is a safety gate, not a performance or translation step. Parsing beats string matching because 'delete' can hide inside a comment or a string.

column3: A manager asks Dining Bot to plan next week. Why hand that to Deep Agents?
column4: Multi-step work needs files and a plan
column5: Open-ended multi-step work needs scratch files, a plan and several passes. Deep Agents may write markdown plans, but still never writes to the database.
column6: RAG and SQL both answer single questions well. Neither is built to produce a multi-day plan, and all three can write text.

column3: Why must AWS credentials never be shipped to the browser?
column4: Anything in client code can be extracted
column5: Anything in client code can be read by any user, including minified JavaScript and network traffic. Privilege has to stay server-side.
column6: CloudFront does not strip secrets for you. The fix is architectural: the browser carries a token, never a credential.

column3: In this stack, what does Cognito establish and what does IAM establish?
column4: Cognito the user, IAM what the server may do
column5: Cognito authenticates the human and issues a JWT. IAM authorises your server to call the agent runtime. Two different questions.
column6: Swapping them is the classic confusion. Identity of the user and permissions of the service are separate concerns.

column3: Your React app calls the agent directly from the browser. What is wrong?
column4: Privilege belongs on the server, not the client
column5: To call the agent you need AWS credentials, and shipping those to the client exposes them. The API must sit in between, verify the JWT, then use its IAM role.
column6: React can certainly make the call technically. The problem is what it would have to hold in order to do so.

column3: On Bedrock AgentCore, what does Gateway provide?
column4: Tools exposed over MCP behind an auth boundary
column5: Gateway exposes tools over MCP behind an auth boundary, so your agent reaches external tools without you hand-rolling the plumbing.
column6: Memory is recall across turns and Runtime is the managed host for the agent. Keep the three primitives distinct, interviewers ask for them by name.

column3: Memory, Runtime and Identity sit in us-east-1 in these labs. Where does Gateway sit?
column4: us-west-2, and mixing them breaks the wiring
column5: Gateway and the Cognito machine-to-machine setup are in us-west-2 in this course. Memory, Runtime and Identity stay in us-east-1.
column6: Assuming one region is the commonest lab failure: memory ids and runtime wiring silently stop resolving. Pass the region explicitly on deploy.

column3: Why define the AWS stack in CDK instead of clicking through the console?
column4: It is reviewable, repeatable and diffable
column5: The stack is code, so it can be reviewed in a pull request, diffed before deploy and recreated identically. That is what makes the CI pipeline possible.
column6: CDK costs the same as clicking, and the console can create everything. The difference is review and repeatability, not capability or price.

column3: Your refund policy changed this morning. RAG or fine-tune?
column4: RAG, update the document and skip training
column5: Facts that change belong in documents. Update the source and the next retrieval is correct, with no training run and no delay.
column6: Fine-tuning to teach a changing fact means retraining every time it changes. Quantization and sampling teach nothing at all.

column3: During LoRA training, what is actually being updated?
column4: Two small matrices, the base stays frozen
column5: The base weights stay frozen. You train two small low-rank matrices whose product is added as the update.
column6: If every weight trained you would be doing full fine-tuning, which needs roughly 112GB for a 7B model instead of a few GB.

column3: For a 512x512 layer at rank 8, how many numbers does LoRA train?
column4: 8,192, about 3% of the full 262,144
column5: B is 512x8 and A is 8x512, so 4,096 + 4,096 = 8,192, against 262,144 for the full matrix. Roughly three percent.
column6: The formula to remember is 2 x d x r, not d squared. Bigger layers make the saving better, not worse.

column3: What does the Q in QLoRA refer to?
column4: The frozen base is quantized to 4-bit
column5: The frozen base model is quantized, typically to 4-bit NF4. The LoRA adapters on top stay at higher precision.
column6: It is the base that gets compressed, not the adapters. That is what drops a 7B base from about 14GB to about 3.5GB.

column3: You quantized a model to 4 bits. Does it now know your internal PDFs?
column4: No, quantization compresses and teaches nothing
column5: Quantization only changes how existing weights are stored. It adds no information, so the model knows exactly what it knew before, slightly less precisely.
column6: Compression is not learning. If you need those PDFs, that is RAG or fine-tuning data, not a bit-width change.

column3: What does LoRA's alpha parameter control?
column4: How strongly the adapter is scaled in
column5: Alpha scales the adapter's contribution, applied as alpha divided by rank. If alpha equals rank the scale is 1.
column6: It does not decide which layers get adapters or set the learning rate. It controls how loudly the adapter speaks.

column3: You need brand voice AND today's prices. What ships?
column4: Fine-tune the voice, retrieve the prices
column5: Fine-tune the behaviour that is stable, retrieve the facts that move. Voice is stable, prices are not.
column6: Nightly fine-tuning to chase prices is expensive and slow. And voice absolutely can be changed, which is what adapters are for.

column3: What does Unsloth give you for a QLoRA run on one Colab GPU?
column4: Faster training and less memory, same recipe
column5: Optimised kernels and memory handling, so the same LoRA or QLoRA recipe trains substantially faster and fits in less VRAM.
column6: It is a speed and memory layer, nothing more. It does not change model size, invent data, or do anything about fresh facts, which remain RAG's job.
